annotations.text:
A — ACADEMIC
Serif display (Newsreader), warm paper background, crimson used sparingly as punctuation. Reads as a credible department site.

Why: ages well, looks legitimate to faculty and prospective sponsors, needs zero photography.
Tradeoff: quiet. Won't grab a freshman scrolling on their phone at the involvement fair.

B — TERMINAL
Dark, monospace, prompts and a log-style event list. Speaks directly to people who already write code.

Why: the most distinctive of the three, and the cheapest to keep looking good — no images to source ever.
Tradeoff: actively filters. A curious business major may read it as 'not for me', which cuts against recruiting.

C — CAMPUS
Bright, rounded, photo-led, recruiting-first. Big claim, membership count, faces.

Why: best at converting newcomers, and the friendliest to non-majors.
Tradeoff: it is only as good as its photos. Every grey [PHOTO] block is a real picture someone has to take and keep taking each year — that is the maintenance burden A and B don't have.

Same content in all three — nav, tagline, Join CTA, three upcoming events, footer. Bracketed values like [##] and [Building & room] are placeholders, not real data. Each artboard has an accent-color chip above it if you want to see it in something other than Samford crimson.
